title: API Design
description: Designing resilient, evolvable, and secure service contracts: RESTful modeling, versioning, cursor pagination, idempotency, rate limiting, gateways, and auth.

subtopics.title: REST API Design
subtopics.subtitle: Resource-oriented noun hierarchies, HTTP method semantics, RFC 7807 error envelopes, and modeling non-CRUD actions.
keyTakeaways: RESTful APIs structure URIs around plural nouns (`/v1/orders`), mapping actions to standard HTTP verbs rather than embedding verbs in endpoints (`/createOrder`).
Non-CRUD actions (such as order cancellation or checkout) are cleanly modeled as state machine transitions or dedicated sub-resources (`POST /orders/{id}/cancellation`).
Long-running operations should return `202 Accepted` immediately with a `Location: /jobs/{id}` status URL and `Retry-After` header to avoid holding open client connections.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
RESTFUL RESOURCE HIERARCHY & ASYNC POLLING PATTERN
CRUD Operations on Collections:
  GET    /api/v1/orders              -> List orders (200 OK)
  POST   /api/v1/orders              -> Create order (201 Created + Location header)
  GET    /api/v1/orders/{orderId}    -> Fetch single order (200 OK / 404 Not Found)
  DELETE /api/v1/orders/{orderId}    -> Cancel/Delete order (204 No Content)

Long-Running Asynchronous Processing:
  POST /api/v1/video-exports         -> 202 Accepted (Location: /api/v1/jobs/j_99)
  GET  /api/v1/jobs/j_99             -> 200 OK (Status: "PROCESSING", Progress: 45%)
  GET  /api/v1/jobs/j_99             -> 303 See Other (Location: /api/v1/downloads/v_99)

sections.heading: Resource Modeling, Nesting Depth, and Non-CRUD Actions
sections.body: A clean REST API models business entities as resources identified by nouns, using HTTP verbs to convey intent. A common mistake is deep URL nesting like `/orgs/{id}/departments/{id}/teams/{id}/members/{id}`, which tightly couples endpoint URLs to internal database foreign key schemas and creates brittle client integrations. In production, nest resources at most one level deep (`/teams/{teamId}/members`); everything else should be queryable by top-level identifiers (`/members/{memberId}`).
bullets: Plural Nouns: Use `/v1/users` and `/v1/accounts`, avoiding RPC-style verbs like `/getUser` or `/deleteAccount`.
Nesting Depth Limit: Keep hierarchy shallow. Use `/orders/{orderId}/items`, but fetch individual line items directly at `/items/{itemId}`.

Non-CRUD State Transitions: When an action doesn't fit standard PUT/PATCH (e.g., executing a checkout or approving a transfer), treat the action as a sub-resource: `POST /orders/{id}/payments` or `POST /transfers/{id}/approval`.

sections.heading: Handling Long-Running Asynchronous Operations
sections.body: HTTP is designed for fast request-response exchanges. When an endpoint triggers a heavy operation like generating a monthly PDF invoice or training a machine learning model, holding the client's HTTP connection open for 45 seconds causes proxy timeouts (504s), connection resets, and client retries that crush backend workers. REST handles this via the `202 Accepted` pattern.
bullets: Admission & 202 Accepted: Validate inputs, enqueue the background job, and immediately return HTTP 202 with a `Location: /jobs/{jobId}` header.
Status Polling: The client polls `/jobs/{jobId}`. While running, the server returns 200 with metadata (`{"status": "in_progress", "progress": 65}`) and a `Retry-After: 5` header.
Completion & Redirection: When finished, the status endpoint returns an HTTP 303 See Other pointing directly to the generated resource (`Location: /invoices/inv_102.pdf`).

tradeOffs.pros: Simpler client integration; client receives final output in one round trip; zero background queue infrastructure required.
tradeOffs.cons: Vulnerable to client and proxy timeouts on slow operations; exhausts server worker threads during traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Simple CRUD operations completing in under 200ms (reading profile, updating address, inserting record).

tradeOffs.pros: Protects API servers from timeouts; decouples work submission from worker fleet execution; absorbs massive traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires clients to manage polling loops or WebSockets; requires persistent job storage to track state.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Video processing, large CSV data exports, report generation, and third-party webhook verification.

subtopics.interviewTip: When designing an API that processes long-running workflows, describe the exact HTTP handoff: 'The API will return a 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to the job status endpoint and a Retry-After header. Once processing completes, the job endpoint returns a 303 See Other redirecting to the completed resource.'

subtopics.title: API Versioning
subtopics.subtitle: Evolving APIs safely without breaking mobile and third-party clients via URI paths, headers, and date-based pinning.
keyTakeaways: Mobile apps cannot be forced to update immediately; production APIs must support older versions concurrently for months or years.
URI path versioning (`/v1/users`) is the most common and transparent strategy; date-based version pinning (Stripe model) offers the cleanest client experience.
Deprecation requires active enforcement: use standard `Sunset` and `Deprecation` HTTP headers and monitor telemetry to identify callers still invoking legacy endpoints.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
API VERSIONING PATTERNS
1. URI PATH VERSIONING (Explicit & CDN-Friendly)
   GET /api/v1/payments/pay_123
   GET /api/v2/payments/pay_123

2. HEADER / DATE-BASED VERSIONING (Stripe Model)
   GET /api/payments/pay_123
   Header: Stripe-Version: 2026-10-03
   (API Gateway transforms internal response using backward-compatibility middleware)

sections.heading: Comparing the Core API Versioning Strategies
sections.body: Once an API is adopted by external developers or native mobile applications, breaking changes cannot simply be deployed in place. Mobile users may not update their app for months. Engineering teams employ three main strategies to evolve contracts while protecting existing clients.
bullets: URI Path Versioning (`/v1/orders`): The version is embedded directly in the path. Simple for developers to understand and easy for CDNs to cache; downside is potential URI bloat and code duplication across controllers.

Header / Accept Versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json`): Keeps URIs clean and permanent, but makes exploratory testing harder with `curl` or in browsers, and requires configuring CDNs to include the `Accept` header in their cache key (`Vary: Accept`).

Date-Based Version Pinning (The Stripe Model): Clients are permanently pinned to the API date when they created their account. The gateway executes bidirectional request/response transformations on top of a single modern internal codebase.

codeSnippet.title: Standard Deprecation Warning Headers in Express/Fastify Middleware

sections.heading: Deprecation Lifecycles and Avoiding Version Sprawl
sections.body: Supporting five different API versions simultaneously slows down engineering velocity and clutters codebases with legacy conditional branches. A mature API program enforces a formal deprecation schedule backed by observability.
bullets: Telemetry on Callers: Log client user-agents, API keys, and account IDs hitting deprecated endpoints; never guess whether a version is still in use.
Proactive Outreach: Email accounts with active traffic on legacy versions 90, 60, and 30 days before sunset.

Brownout Testing: Intentionally inject intermittent HTTP 410 Gone responses for 15-minute windows during non-peak hours weeks before the sunset deadline to identify forgotten cron jobs before permanent teardown.

tradeOffs.pros: Obvious to developers; works seamlessly in web browsers and Postman; CDN edge caching is trivial without header variance.
tradeOffs.cons: Can lead to duplicated controller code; encourages bumping entire API versions for changes to a single endpoint.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Public developer platforms, mobile app backends, and microservice boundary contracts.

tradeOffs.pros: Single codebase internally; changes are isolated to request/response schema transformer layers; ideal developer experience.
tradeOffs.cons: High engineering investment to build and maintain the bidirectional mutation pipeline.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Enterprise developer-first SaaS platforms with thousands of mission-critical third-party integrations.

subtopics.interviewTip: When asked how to handle a breaking API change, emphasize backward compatibility first: 'Whenever possible, avoid bumping versions by adding optional fields rather than removing or renaming existing fields. If a breaking change is mandatory, introduce `/v2` alongside `/v1`, emit standard `Sunset` HTTP headers, and monitor API-key-level telemetry to track migration progress.'

subtopics.title: Pagination
subtopics.subtitle: Why Offset/Limit pagination breaks at scale, and how Keyset/Cursor pagination guarantees O(1) index seeking.
keyTakeaways: Offset pagination (`OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20`) forces relational database engines to scan and discard 100,000 index rows, causing query latency to spike linearly with page depth.
Offset pagination suffers from page drift: if a new row is inserted while a user navigates between pages, they will observe duplicate items on the next page.
Keyset (Cursor) pagination uses indexed ordering columns (`WHERE (created_at, id) < ($cursor_time, $cursor_id)`) to seek directly to the next page in O(1) time.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
PAGINATION MECHANICS: OFFSET VS CURSOR
OFFSET PAGINATION (Linear O(N) Scan Overhead):
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000;
[ Disk Read ] -> Reads and discards 500,000 rows -> Returns 20 rows (Slow! High IOPS)

CURSOR PAGINATION (Direct O(log N) B-Tree Seek):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-01', 9942) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
[ B-Tree Index ] -> Jumps straight to leaf pointer -> Reads 20 rows immediately (Sub-5ms!)

sections.heading: The Two Fatal Flaws of Offset Pagination at Scale
sections.body: Offset pagination (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000`) is simple to implement and maps cleanly to UI pagination controls ('Jump to Page 500'). However, in production databases, it introduces two severe failure modes.
bullets: Linear Performance Collapse: Databases cannot jump directly to row 100,000 on disk. The storage engine must traverse the B-Tree index, fetch 100,020 rows, discard the first 100,000 in memory, and return the remaining 20. On tables with millions of rows, deep pages take seconds to execute and saturate database IOPS.

Page Drift / Data Inconsistency: If an infinite-scroll mobile feed uses offset pagination and 5 new posts are published while the user views page 1, requesting page 2 (`OFFSET 20`) causes the last 5 posts from page 1 to shift down into page 2, presenting the user with duplicate records.

sections.heading: Engineering Bulletproof Cursor Pagination
sections.body: Cursor pagination works by pointing to a specific record and asking the database for items that occur strictly before or after that point. By anchoring queries on an indexed column (or composite key), the database performs a sub-millisecond B-Tree index seek regardless of whether you are on the 1st page or the 10,000th page.
bullets: Tie-Breaking with Unique Columns: Timestamps alone are not unique; multiple records created in the same millisecond cause skipping or duplicates. Always use a composite cursor: `(created_at, id)`.
Opaque Cursors: Never expose raw database column values directly in client API contracts. Base64-encode or encrypt cursor payloads so client code treats the cursor as an opaque token.

The Usability Trade-off: Cursor pagination does not support jumping directly to arbitrary pages ('Go to Page 42') or calculating total pages. It is specifically optimized for infinite scroll feeds, chat histories, and export streams.

tradeOffs.pros: Trivial to implement in SQL; allows jumping directly to arbitrary page numbers; supports total page counts.
tradeOffs.cons: O(N) database latency on deep pages; causes duplicate items and missed items during active concurrent writes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal admin panels with small datasets (<10,000 rows) requiring direct page jump navigation.

tradeOffs.pros: Deterministic O(1) performance regardless of table depth; completely immune to page drift and duplicate items.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot jump directly to arbitrary page numbers; sorting requires matching composite database indexes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-scale public APIs, social media timelines, chat message history, and infinite-scroll mobile feeds.

subtopics.interviewTip: When asked to design a feed or message history endpoint, immediately specify cursor pagination over offset pagination: 'We will use cursor-based pagination backed by a composite index on `(created_at, id)`. This prevents duplicate feed items as new posts arrive and maintains sub-10ms lookup times even on deep pages.'

subtopics.title: Idempotency
subtopics.subtitle: Guaranteeing exactly-once execution over at-least-once networks using Idempotency-Key headers and atomic state locks.
keyTakeaways: Over unreliable networks, a timeout does not mean a request failed; it often means the server processed the operation, but the response dropped on the return path.
Idempotency keys (e.g., `Idempotency-Key: <UUID>`) allow clients to retry mutations safely without duplicating financial transactions or inventory deductions.
An idempotency store must handle three states: pending execution (return 409 or wait), completed execution (return cached response), and failed execution (allow retry).
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
IDEMPOTENCY KEY EXECUTION FLOW
[ Client ] --- POST /v1/charges (Idempotency-Key: "uuid-99") ---> [ Payment API ]
                                                                       |
                                              +------------------------+
                                              | Check Redis / DB Key
                                              v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Case 1: First Time -> Set key="PROCESSING" (with TTL) -> Process DB  |
| Case 2: In-Flight  -> Key is "PROCESSING" -> Return 409 Conflict     |
| Case 3: Completed  -> Return cached HTTP 201 + Original Body         |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: Why Retries Are Unsafe Without Idempotency Keys
sections.body: Distributed systems operate over at-least-once networks where packet loss is normal. When a client submits a POST request to charge a credit card and the connection times out after 10 seconds, the client cannot know whether the server never received the request, crashed mid-execution, or succeeded completely and dropped the HTTP 200 response on the return wire. If the client retries naively, it risks charging the customer twice.
bullets: The Two Generals Problem in Practice: You cannot guarantee delivery confirmation over an unreliable channel without acknowledgments.
Client-Generated UUIDs: The client generates a unique idempotency key before initiating the request and includes it in the `Idempotency-Key` header.
Server-Side Cache: The server stores the idempotency key along with the original response body and HTTP status code for a bounded TTL (e.g., 24 to 72 hours).

sections.heading: Transactional Idempotency in Databases and Message Queues
sections.body: While in-memory caches like Redis work well for edge API idempotency, core financial engines enforce idempotency at the database storage layer. By inserting the idempotency key into a dedicated SQL table with a unique constraint within the same transaction that updates balances, duplicate operations are rejected atomically by the database engine.
bullets: Unique Database Constraints: `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, user_id, status)` will trigger an immediate unique-key violation on duplicate submissions.
Kafka Consumer Idempotency: Message consumers must track processed message IDs or write outputs to storage using upsert keys (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) to handle at-least-once message redeliveries.
Payload Hashing: Advanced idempotency implementations hash the request body alongside the key to reject requests where a client reuses an idempotency key with different parameters.

tradeOffs.pros: Sub-millisecond verification latency; offloads lock checks from primary relational databases; automatic key expiration via TTLs.
tradeOffs.cons: If Redis fails or restarts without persistence, in-flight idempotency locks could be lost.
tradeOffs.bestFor: API Gateways, public web/mobile endpoints, and distributed microservice edge ingress.

tradeOffs.pros: Strict ACID durability; transactionally coupled with business balance changes; zero risk of lock loss during failovers.
tradeOffs.cons: Adds write IOPS and table bloat to primary database; requires background jobs to prune old keys.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Payment ledgers, banking transfers, inventory reservations, and billing settlement engines.

subtopics.interviewTip: Whenever designing payment processing, ticket booking, or e-commerce orders, introduce an Idempotency-Key header upfront: 'To make retries safe over unreliable networks, the API will require an Idempotency-Key header. We will store this key and the resulting response in Redis with a 24-hour TTL, ensuring duplicate requests return the original outcome without double-charging.'

subtopics.title: Rate Limiting
subtopics.subtitle: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window algorithms, and distributed atomic enforcement using Redis Lua scripts.
keyTakeaways: Rate limiting protects backend systems from denial-of-service spikes, brute-force credential stuffing, and noisy-neighbor resource starvation.
The Token Bucket algorithm allows controlled bursts while enforcing an average rate; the Sliding Window Counter algorithm prevents 2x boundary spikes with minimal memory.
In distributed architectures, rate limit checks must execute atomically in Redis using single Lua scripts to prevent read-modify-write race conditions.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
DISTRIBUTED RATE LIMITING AT THE EDGE GATEWAY
[ Client Requests ]
        |
        v
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                   API Gateway Edge                    |
| - Extracts Client Identifier (API Key, User ID, IP)   |
| - Executes Atomic Lua Script on Redis Cluster         |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+
                            |
           EVAL "redis_sliding_window.lua" (1 RTT)
                            v
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                 Redis Cluster / Shard                 |
|  Allowed? -> Yes: Forward to Microservices            |
|  Allowed? -> No:  Return HTTP 429 + Retry-After: 12   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: Comparing the Core Rate Limiting Algorithms
sections.body: Selecting a rate limiting algorithm depends on whether your workload requires smoothing traffic out into an even trickle or accommodating brief, legitimate bursts of client activity.
bullets: Token Bucket: Tokens accumulate in a bucket at a steady rate up to a maximum capacity. Each request consumes one token. If empty, the request is rejected. Ideal for APIs that must tolerate natural client bursts while capping long-term throughput.

Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a FIFO queue and leak out at a constant, fixed rate. Flattens out bursts completely; excess requests overflow and drop. Best for queue-based worker protection and traffic shaping.

Fixed Window: Counts requests in fixed time windows (e.g., 100 requests per minute from 12:00 to 12:01). Severe flaw: a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 requests at 12:01:01, dumping 200 requests within two seconds (2x burst spike).

Sliding Window Counter: Calculates an estimated count by taking the current window's count plus a weighted percentage of the previous window. Delivers 99%+ accuracy with tiny memory footprint (two integer keys per user).

codeSnippet.title: Atomic Sliding Window Rate Limiter via Redis Lua Script
codeSnippet.code:
-- KEYS[1]: rate limit key (e.g., 'ratelimit:user_123')
-- ARGV[1]: current timestamp in milliseconds
-- ARGV[2]: window size in milliseconds (e.g., 60000 for 1 minute)
-- ARGV[3]: max allowed requests in window

local key = KEYS[1]
local now = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local clearBefore = now - window

-- 1. Remove timestamps outside the sliding window
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, clearBefore)

-- 2. Count remaining requests in the active window
local currentRequests = redis.call('ZCARD', key)

if currentRequests < limit then
  -- 3. Add current request and reset key expiration
  redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now)
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
  return 1 -- Allowed
else
  return 0 -- Rejected (Rate limit exceeded)
end

sections.heading: Distributed Rate Limiting and Informative Client Headers
sections.body: In a multi-server deployment, rate limits cannot be stored in local server memory because requests from the same user land on different servers behind the load balancer. Storing counts in a centralized Redis cluster solves this, but naive client implementations that read a count, increment it, and write it back create race conditions under high concurrency. Atomic Lua scripts guarantee thread safety in a single round trip.
bullets: Standard Client Headers: Transparent APIs inform callers of their quota via `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset`.
Handling Rejections: Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests paired with a `Retry-After: <seconds>` header so well-behaved clients back off without hammering the endpoint.
Tiered Enforcement: Apply multiple rate limits simultaneously (e.g., 10 requests per second for burst protection, paired with 5,000 requests per day for billing compliance).

tradeOffs.pros: Supports natural bursty traffic while bounding average throughput; memory footprint is tiny (just token count and timestamp).
tradeOffs.cons: Allows bursts that can temporarily stress downstream microservices if burst capacity is configured too generously.
tradeOffs.bestFor: General public APIs (AWS, GitHub, Stripe), user authentication endpoints, and payment gateways.

tradeOffs.pros: Smooths outgoing traffic into a perfectly steady flow; eliminates downstream database spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Holds requests in memory queues, increasing latency for bursts; drops packets if queue overflows.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Asynchronous job queues, outgoing email/SMS delivery pipelines, and network packet shaping.

subtopics.interviewTip: Whenever an interviewer asks where rate limiting should live, recommend enforcing it at the API Gateway layer using Redis with Lua scripts: 'Enforcing rate limits at the gateway prevents unauthorized or excessive traffic from consuming compute resources in internal microservices, and using Lua scripts avoids race conditions without distributed locks.'

subtopics.title: API Gateway
subtopics.subtitle: Centralizing edge concerns: TLS termination, JWT validation, rate limiting, routing, and the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern.
keyTakeaways: An API Gateway serves as the single public entry point for client traffic, centralizing cross-cutting concerns like TLS, authentication, and rate limiting.
The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern deploys dedicated gateways tailored to specific client platforms (iOS, Android, Web), preventing bloated one-size-fits-all payloads.
API Gateways must avoid accumulating business domain logic; gateways should focus on routing, telemetry, and protocol translation, leaving domain logic to internal services.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
BACKEND-FOR-FRONTEND (BFF) GATEWAY TOPOLOGY
[ Web Clients ]         [ Mobile iOS/Android ]         [ Third-Party APIs ]
       |                          |                               |
       v                          v                               v
[ Web BFF Gateway ]     [ Mobile BFF Gateway ]         [ Public Edge Gateway ]
(Desktop Aggregation)   (Compact JSON / Protobuf)      (Strict Rate Limiting & Auth)
       |                          |                               |
       +--------------------------+-------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
            [ Internal East-West Microservices Mesh ]
            (Auth Service, Order Service, Inventory Service)

sections.heading: Core Responsibilities of the Edge Gateway
sections.body: Exposing internal microservices directly to the public internet creates major security vulnerabilities, tight coupling, and excessive network round trips. An API Gateway sits between external clients and internal services, terminating connections and handling shared operational concerns.
bullets: Edge Security & Auth: Terminates TLS, validates incoming JWT tokens or API keys, and drops unauthorized traffic before it touches internal networks.
Rate Limiting & DDoS Shielding: Enforces token bucket or sliding window limits per IP or account, protecting downstream services from saturation.
Protocol Transcoding: Accepts external JSON/REST or WebSockets from browsers and translates them into internal gRPC calls over HTTP/2.
Correlation & Tracing: Injects a unique `X-Request-ID` or W3C `traceparent` header into every inbound request, ensuring end-to-end distributed trace visibility.

codeSnippet.title: API Gateway Reverse Proxy Route Definition (Envoy / KrakenD style)
codeSnippet.code:
endpoint: "/api/v1/user-dashboard"
method: "GET"
output_encoding: "json"
backend:
  - url_pattern: "/internal/v1/users/{user_id}"
    method: "GET"
    host: "http://user-service:8080"
  - url_pattern: "/internal/v1/orders/recent?user={user_id}"
    method: "GET"
    host: "http://order-service:8080"
# Concurrently queries user and order services and merges payloads into a single response

sections.heading: The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Pattern
sections.body: A desktop browser on high-speed fiber has different requirements than a mobile phone on a spotty cellular connection. Building a single generic API forces mobile clients to make multiple network calls to gather dashboard data, while receiving oversized JSON payloads packed with desktop-only fields. The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern creates specialized edge gateways for each client category.
bullets: Mobile BFF: Aggregates multiple backend RPC calls into a single response; strips unnecessary fields to conserve mobile bandwidth; compresses payloads.
Web BFF: Delivers rich relational payloads tailored for large screens; handles server-side rendering (SSR) session hydration.

The Antipattern of the 'Smart Gateway': Never embed business logic, database transactions, or business rules into the gateway. Gateways should remain thin routing and orchestration proxies; when gateways become bloated with domain code, they turn into monolithic bottlenecks.

tradeOffs.pros: Single operational boundary to manage; uniform security and rate limiting policies; straightforward deployment.
tradeOffs.cons: Becomes an organizational bottleneck if multiple teams fight over routing configuration; one-size-fits-all payload compromises.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-to-mid stage startups with uniform client requirements and smaller engineering teams.

tradeOffs.pros: Frontend teams own their respective gateways; optimal network payloads and latency per client platform; independent release cycles.
tradeOffs.cons: Operational overhead of maintaining multiple gateway fleets; potential duplication of edge authentication boilerplate.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large engineering organizations with dedicated mobile, web, and public platform teams.

subtopics.interviewTip: In mobile-heavy system design problems (like Uber or Instagram), bring up the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern: 'To optimize for lossy mobile networks, we will place a Mobile BFF Gateway between the mobile app and internal services. It aggregates multiple microservice calls into a single response and trims unneeded fields to save cellular bandwidth.'

subtopics.title: Authentication / Authorization
subtopics.subtitle: Distinguishing AuthN from AuthZ, stateless JWTs vs stateful sessions, OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, and RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC.
keyTakeaways: Authentication (AuthN) verifies who the user is; Authorization (AuthZ) verifies what resources and actions the user is permitted to access.
Stateless JWTs eliminate database lookups at the cost of difficult revocation; stateful sessions in Redis allow instant revocation but require a network hop on every request.
Access control models evolve from simple Role-Based (RBAC) to Attribute-Based (ABAC) and finally Relationship-Based (ReBAC, Google Zanzibar) for collaborative graph permissions.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
STATELESS JWT VS STATEFUL REDIS SESSION
STATELESS JWT (Zero DB Lookups, Hard Revocation):
[ Client ] --- Bearer <JWT> ---> [ App Server ]
                                        |
                       Cryptographic Signature Verified via Public Key
                       (No DB or Cache lookup required!)

STATEFUL SESSION (Instant Revocation, Centralized Store):
[ Client ] --- Cookie: sid_98124 ---> [ App Server ]
                                             |
                                  Query Redis: GET sid_98124
                                             v
                                    [ Redis Cluster ]

sections.heading: Stateless JWTs vs Stateful Sessions and Revocation
sections.body: Session management fundamentally trades off verification latency against revocation control. Traditional web applications store a session ID in a cookie and keep the user's session state in a centralized Redis cluster. Modern microservice architectures often favor JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which are cryptographically signed payloads verified locally by any service using an asymmetric public key.
bullets: Stateful Sessions: When a user changes their password or an administrator bans an account, deleting the session key in Redis instantly logs out the user worldwide. Downside: every single API request must perform a Redis lookup.

Stateless JWTs: Services verify the cryptographic signature locally without querying a central database, making them fast and horizontally scalable. Downside: once issued, a JWT is valid until its expiration timestamp (`exp`). Revoking a compromised token before expiration requires maintaining a revocation blocklist in memory.

The Production Hybrid: Use short-lived JWT access tokens (10-15 minute expiry) paired with long-lived stateful refresh tokens (7-30 days) stored in the database. When the access token expires, the client exchanges the refresh token, allowing the server to enforce bans or permission changes.

sections.heading: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC
sections.body: Once identity is proven, the authorization engine determines whether the actor can perform the requested operation on the target resource. As applications grow in complexity, permission models evolve through three distinct architectures.
bullets: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Users are assigned roles (`Admin`, `Editor`, `Viewer`), and roles have static permissions. Simple to manage, but breaks down when permissions depend on context ('Can an Editor edit a document owned by another department?').

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC): Evaluates dynamic attributes of the user, the resource, and the environment (e.g., 'Allow access if User.Department == Resource.Department AND Request.Time < 18:00'). Highly flexible, but complex to audit and evaluate efficiently.

Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC): Pioneered by Google's Zanzibar paper. Permissions are modeled as a graph of relationships (e.g., 'User A is a member of Team B, which owns Folder C, which contains Document D'). Evaluated using high-speed distributed graph traversals.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero database lookups on request paths; microservices verify tokens independently using public keys; scales seamlessly.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot revoke tokens immediately without maintaining a distributed blocklist; larger payload size over the wire.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput microservice ecosystems, mobile application APIs, and federated Single Sign-On (SSO).

tradeOffs.pros: Instant token revocation across all devices; session metadata can be updated in real time; compact cookie tokens.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a network round trip to Redis on every single request; session store is a critical dependency for uptime.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic web apps, administrative banking portals, and sensitive internal enterprise applications.

subtopics.interviewTip: When discussing authentication in microservices, suggest the short-lived JWT + refresh token pattern: 'We issue short-lived 10-minute JWT access tokens verified locally by microservices without database queries, paired with long-lived refresh tokens checked against a database only once every 10 minutes to verify revocation status.'
